item.title: Would Your Employees Join a Fake Anthropic AI Preview?
item.description: Cofense Intelligence has identified a credential phishing campaign that exploits interest in emerging AI technology by sending fake invitations to an exclusive Anthropic AI preview. Threat actors abuse legitimate services, URL shorteners, and multiple CAPTCHAs to bypass traditional email security defenses and redirect victims to convincing Google and Microsoft login pages designed to steal credentials.
item.content:encoded:
By: Intelligence Team, Jacob Malimban

Since September 2026, threat actors have been sending emails that appear to be an invitation to a private Anthropic AI meeting, but are actually attempts to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials. Exclusive access to new AI technology is valuable to many organizations, which is why threat actors use it as a lure in their phishing emails. 

Risks to the organization from this campaign include threat actors compromising a sensitive account, accessing the account’s sensitive documents (e.g. proprietary marketing material), and using the compromised account as an initial vector to further infiltrate the organization. Employees must stay vigilant, as these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies due to the abuse of legitimate tools like URL shorteners and CAPTCHAs. 

Cofense Intelligence consolidates campaign data, including indicators of compromise (IOCs) such as malicious web addresses, phishing email content, and broader campaign context, into Active Threat Reports (ATRs), providing a comprehensive view of identified threats. ATRs contain the full infection chain from the initial phishing link to the final malware file or credential phishing resource. If one ATR IOC appears in the organization, cybersecurity professionals can read the ATR to understand the phishing attack’s impact and mitigations. Each ATR has been curated by a human analyst. This human-vetted intelligence provides context and the campaign information necessary to mitigate future phishing attacks. For this private Anthropic AI preview campaign, actionable intelligence can be found in ATRs 423868, 423866, and 423475.

Key Points

  • The campaign contains a tantalizing, private offer to preview Anthropic AI technology, which may be enough for employees to click before inspecting the email.
  • The video teleconference software GoTo Webinar, which is used to send legitimate meeting emails and is usually not blocked by email security technologies, was abused to send a threat actor’s URL instead.
  • The URL shortener zpr[.]io, which turns long URLs into short links, has been abused to help these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies. 
  • CAPTCHAs, which are tests that confirm a real human is visiting the website, are similarly abused to prevent automated analysis.
  • Threat actors use subdomains and dashes (-) to obfuscate the malicious URL.

Step 1: The Invitation Email 

Figure 1: Anthropic meeting invitation email used in credential phishing (ATR 423475).

Emails in this campaign claim to be an exclusive invitation to see Anthropic’s new AI tool. Many organizations are deciding how AI fits into their business, so a private preview would be very valuable if the email were real. As developments in AI continue to dominate the news cycle, getting a private preview of advancements in Anthropic’s AI is an effective phishing lure.

The phishing email appears to be an abuse of the legitimate GoTo Webinar service. The email sender address appears to be customercare@gotowebinar[.]com. Threat actors have previously abused that email address and GoTo Webinar’s free trial in 2020. The email also contains a footer with GoTo Webinar branding.

The text in the email contains no obvious spelling errors. The email sender name, however, reads “Austin from nthropic” with the “A” missing from Anthropic. Although this is a small misspelling, it is still a useful warning sign.

The link in the email appears to be generated by Zapier’s URL shortener service. Zapier is a legitimate business process automation company, and their URL Shortener is designed to work with Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible AI. Unfortunately, this tool has been abused by threat actors during this Anthropic AI Preview campaign. In other campaigns, threat actors have abused non-AI, trusted services like link shorteners or cloud collaboration platforms as the first link in a phishing campaign to avoid being blocked by email security technologies.

Step 2: The First Checkpoint

Figure 2: Cloudflare CAPTCHA page to hinder automated analysis (ATR 423868).

If the phishing email link is clicked, a CAPTCHA page appears. This Cloudflare CAPTCHA must be completed before the phishing content is shown. This CAPTCHA is the first of two checkpoints that help threat actors block automated scans of their website. Because CAPTCHAs are common on legitimate websites, phishing recipients may believe all is well and everything is secure because of the CAPTCHA.

Step 3: The Fake Meeting Page

Figure 3: Zoom-spoofing page with Anthropic meeting information (ATR 423475).

After completing the CAPTCHA, a Zoom-spoofing meeting invitation page appears. This brand does not match the GoTo Webinar branding from the email. The page’s Zoom branding is consistent with the “zoom” in the malicious domain, us968web-zoom[.]us.

If the phishing recipient wants to attend the “meeting”, they need to register for the event. They are prompted to register with their work email. Credential phishing occurs when the user clicks on either “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”.

Step 4: The Second Checkpoint

Figure 4: Custom CAPTCHA page to further hinder automated analysis (ATR 423475).

After clicking “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”, another CAPTCHA page appears. This CAPTCHA requires a sliding motion to “unlock” the page. This custom CAPTCHA also appears to be good at detecting and blocking analysis from the most popular VPN services, scanners, Tor browser, and other tools used by defenders.

Because the phishing attack has two distinct CAPTCHAs, automated analysis tools may not be able to follow every step in the credential phishing attack.

Step 5A: The Fake Google Login Page

Figure 5: Google credential phishing page after custom CAPTCHA (ATR 423866).

If “Continue with Google” is clicked and the CAPTCHA is completed, the Google credential phishing page appears. Currently, the Google credential phishing page only captures usernames. It is likely that the page is misconfigured as it does not prompt for a password. After credentials are submitted, the browser does not redirect to the real Google login page, nor does a fake confirmation appear. 

Not only is the phishing page remarkably similar to the legitimate Google login page, but the subdomain is also tricky. Employees who quickly read goo[.]gle-access-eventregister[.]icu might not recognize that the URL is not Google. 

Step 5B: The Fake Microsoft Login Page

Figure 6: Microsoft credential phishing page after custom CAPTCHA (ATR 423475).

If instead of clicking on “Continue with Google”, the user clicked “Continue with Microsoft”, the Microsoft credential phishing page would load. Just like the previous Google Credential Phishing section, the CAPTCHA must be completed (Figure 4) before the phishing content is shown. Unlike the Google credential phishing page, the Microsoft version captures both the username and password. After credentials are submitted, the browser does not redirect to the real Microsoft login page, nor does a fake confirmation appear.

The Microsoft phishing page mimics the real Microsoft login page well. It also has a tricky subdomain, where office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com mimics the real office[.]com or sharepoint[.]com domain. Entering credentials into this page exfiltrates them to the threat actor.

Conclusion

This report covers the private Anthropic AI Preview campaign that uses a fake invitation lure, multiple CAPTCHAs, and Google and Microsoft login page replicas. The campaign was very likely designed by threat actors to bypass current email security technologies and tools used by defenders. Once the employee has reached the credential phishing page, they may not be looking for warning signs anymore. The Google credential phishing page only targets usernames, whereas the Microsoft credential phishing page asks for both the username and password. Stolen credentials give threat actors access to a trusted account, the emails stored in it, and a foothold for future attacks against the organization.

Mitigations

  • Check if the brand remains consistent from the email to a login page. Although organizations can use services like GoTo Webinar to send meetings on their behalf, a GoTo Webinar email is unlikely to redirect to a Zoom event registration page. Searching for small inconsistencies can help identify an email as part of a phishing campaign.
  • Remind employees that both the URL and domain determine whether a login page is legitimate. Although the logos and design of the page may look correct, threat actors are skilled at mimicry especially now with the use of AI. Note that the URL in the email might not be the same URL as the login page due to URL redirects.
  • Use Cofense Vision. Vision AI can cluster structurally related messages even when threat actors rotate senders, subjects, URLs, and page elements.
  • Invest in human-vetted threat intelligence to complement automated feeds. Automated systems are fast but cannot always tell the difference between a legitimate tool being used by IT and the same tool being abused by threat actors, and human analysis adds the context and confidence that AI-based speed cannot provide.

To learn how Cofense combines AI-driven detection, human-vetted threat intelligence, and rapid remediation to identify and stop sophisticated phishing attacks that bypass traditional security defenses, visit cofense.com/platform.

item.title: Locked and Loaded: Phishing through Fake Bids and Protected Documents
item.description: In this blog, Cofense Phishing Defence Centre analyst Don Santos examines a credential phishing campaign that uses fake project bid invitations and password-protected PDFs to create a sense of legitimacy while evading email security detection. Once opened, the PDF directs recipients to a fraudulent document-sharing platform that ultimately leads to a fake Microsoft login page designed to steal their credentials. The campaign highlights how threat actors exploit familiar business processes and trusted platforms, reinforcing the importance of verifying unexpected requests, suspicious links, and login pages before sharing sensitive information.
item.content:encoded:
By Don Santos, Cofense Phishing Defence Centre

In the sales process, few emails carry as much weight as an invitation to bid. It opens the conversation that can eventually lead to revenue, and professionals are conditioned to treat it with urgency and care. Threat actors understand this, and they have learned to pair that urgency with a simple tactic: the password-protected document. Password protection lends the file an air of legitimacy, mimicking a practice companies use every day, while providing threat actors with a critical advantage - most email security tools cannot inspect the contents of an encrypted file. In this walkthrough, we break down how an important sales invitation and a "secured" document combine to set up a tricky and deceptive credential phishing campaign.
 


Figure 1: Invite to Bid Email Body
 

The campaign starts with an email titled "Project Bid Invitation - Proposal Due August 35, 2026" as shown above in Figure 1. The subject and opening message immediately signal good news: an invitation to bid for a new project. The prospect of new business has a way of lowering an employee's guard because it often encourages a sense of urgency, not scepticism. The message says more details are in the password protected PDF attachment. This is another factor that makes the campaign tricky, as it’s a simple yet remarkably effective tactic for evading suspicion. It builds a false sense of trust with the recipient, and more importantly, it allows suspicious URLs or payloads to evade detection from automated email security tools. These tools typically work by scanning a file’s contents for suspicious patterns, but encryption keeps that content unreadable until a password is manually entered, letting the payload bypass detection entirely. Invitations to bid and password-protected files are also used in legitimate business processes, imitating these makes it difficult for untrained employees to spot suspicious emails, as shown in Figure 1. Adding to the difficulty is the fact that the sender's email address itself may belong to a legitimate, previously compromised account rather than an obviously spoofed or unfamiliar domain. This adds another layer of trust, removing one of the most apparent red flags before the recipient even opens the message.
 


Figure 2: Inside the Password Protected PDF
 

If the recipient does proceed with opening the attached PDF and unlocking it, the file reveals content as shown in Figure 2: a single button styled to resemble a OneDrive document preview, prompting them to "View" or "Download" the project files. With only one possible action, there is no room for ambiguity, and the familiar OneDrive branding makes the next click feel valid and legitimate. Hovering over the button reveals the underlying URL, [hXXps://slotpastimaxwin50jt[.]online/autoproject@autoproject[.]com/index[.]php], a clear red flag, as this is not a OneDrive domain, but a redirecting URL designed to carry the recipient further into the campaign. 



Figure 3: Fake Bid Document Drive
 

Clicking the View/Download button leads to a page that resembles a shared document drive, complete with a list of files that appear to be related to a real contract, as shown above in Figure 3. This displays an effort to be consistent with the "invitation to bid" narrative, keeping the intended target hooked and committed to see the process through. Just like a legitimate shared document page, the intended target can choose which files to download via checkbox, then click "Download Selected", continuing the illusion of a normal bid process.
 

Figure 4: Email Input Required
 

Once the "Download Selected" button is clicked, a pop-up window appears asking for an email address, as seen in Figure 4. This again mimics the behaviour of real shared document platforms, which often request a login email to confirm that only the intended recipient can access the file. Entering an email to continue redirects to the fake Microsoft login, closely resembling the real Microsoft sign-in, first asking for an email, then a password, as shown in Figure 5. Looking at the address bar reveals the URL [hXXps://mm-lasertechnik[.]lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/1Dmw9/?key=NKsIDYXvtY], a clear indication that the victim is not on a real Microsoft sign-in page. If the victim proceeds to enter their email and password here, the credentials are sent directly to the attacker's server [hXXps://nbpn[.]lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/nasa[.]php], completing the phish.
 


Figure 5: Fake Microsoft Login Page
 

This campaign shows how threat actors continue to weaponize everyday business processes such as invitations to bid, password-protected files, and shared document platforms, turning them into effective phishing campaigns. The best defence is a habit of caution at every stage: Was this bid expected? Does the sender's domain check out? Does the URL of the login page match the platform it claims to be? When something feels off, contact your IT or security team before entering any credentials, as a moment of caution costs far less than a compromised account. Cofense combines phishing-specific AI trained on expert-validated, real-world intelligence with campaign-level remediation. Once a threat is confirmed, analyst-controlled quarantine can extend across the related campaign, with explainable decisions and a full audit trail. Schedule a demonstration to see how Cofense helps stop trusted-brand credential phishing after it gets through.

item.title: Threats Hidden in Replies: Threat Actors Deliver Malware and Credential Phishing in Email Threads
item.description: Recently, threat actors have been increasingly delivering malware or credential phishing attacks at the end of long email threads designed to exploit a potential victim’s trust in an email contact. In this tactic, threat actors deliver malicious payloads at the end of seemingly normal email conversations after gaining the potential victim’s trust. These kinds of attacks, also known as email thread hijacking, exploit the recipient’s trust in the sender after several legitimate emails.
item.content:encoded:
By: Intelligence Team, Kahng An

Recently, threat actors have been increasingly delivering malware or credential phishing attacks at the end of long email threads designed to exploit a potential victim’s trust in an email contact. In this tactic, threat actors deliver malicious payloads at the end of seemingly normal email conversations after gaining the potential victim’s trust. These kinds of attacks, also known as email thread hijacking, exploit the recipient’s trust in the sender after several legitimate emails. Often these are legitimate email threads that threat actors respond to when accessing compromised email accounts. However, they can also be email threads intentionally started by the threat actor. In these latter cases, the emails start off as seemingly harmless messages that are used to build trust with a potential victim before delivering a malicious threat. While Cofense Intelligence has been tracking these campaigns as response-themed emails, the actual malicious email at the end of the thread is usually similar to simpler meeting invitation, document, or shared file-themed emails. As such, properly trained and aware recipients should be able to spot these threats that are embedded at the end of a conversation. This report is a high-level overview of some recent response-themed emails and some common campaign patterns to be aware of.

Key Points

  • Threat actors have been found delivering malware or credential phishing attacks as replies to email threads. These email replies can be found in both existing legitimate email threads and ones started by the threat actor.
    • Cofense Intelligence tracks these campaigns as response-themed Active Threat Reports (ATR), which outline the campaign’s spoofed brands, subject lines, and resulting malicious payloads.
    • Response-themed ATRs focus on IOCs (indicators of compromise) from the final malicious reply in an email thread.
  • Response-themed emails can be difficult to filter against because they are found within email threads that contain mostly non-malicious messages. Traditional email security solutions may trust long threads of seemingly legitimate emails and fail to block the final malicious payload.
  • Malware delivery was the predominant threat in Q1 2026 with 83.3% of response-themed ATRs being malware ATRs, but credential phishing was more prevalent in Q2 and Q3 2026 with 62.5% and 92.1% of total response-themed ATR volume in those quarters.
  • While response-themed emails have been increasing in popularity this year, response-themed emails are not a completely new tactic. They were previously seen in similar volume in Q1 2024 though were rarely seen by Cofense Intelligence throughout all the latter half of 2024 and almost all of 2025.

What Are Response-Themed Emails?

Cofense Intelligence tracks response-themed emails as any malicious emails that appear to be, or actually are, a reply to an email thread. These kinds of threats are notable because the vast majority of malicious emails are messages that are not contained within a thread. By delivering malware or phishing sites within replies to an email thread, threat actors are able to abuse pre-established trust that was formed over a series of seemingly legitimate back-and-forth messages. The ultimate goal of response-themed email campaigns is to establish a higher level of trust with a potential victim over a series of message replies (or abuse already established trust from a pre-existing email thread) and betray that trust with a standard malicious email lure. In short, response-themed emails are not necessarily any different from the typical malicious email except for this additional abuse of trust and the amount of time the threat actor devotes to developing this trust.

While the concept may seem basic, response-themed emails tend to be rarer compared to most other email themes. This is largely because replying within email threads requires a threat actor to either opportunistically use an existing email chain within a compromised account or intentionally target potential victims with seemingly legitimate email correspondence. These factors lead response-themed campaigns to be rarer and generally more targeted. Figure 1 shows the frequency of response-themed ATRs from Q1 2024 to Q3 2026.

Figure 1: Frequency of response-themed ATRs from Q1 2024 to Q3 2026.

The recent volume of response-themed emails is not unprecedented. Q1 2024 saw a similar amount of total response-themed email campaign volume to what was seen in Q2 2026. However, the majority of campaign threats during this time were credential phishing attacks instead of malware delivery. Response-themed emails quickly plummeted in volume after Q1 2024 and were not seen in any substantial volume until Q1 2026. From there, the quarterly volume of response-themed malware ATRs has remained relatively stable until Q3 2026, while the amount of credential phishing ATRs has continuously skyrocketed in Q2 and Q3 2026.

Campaign Characteristics

Generally, response-themed emails are only distinguished by the fact that they are malicious emails within email threads. While these kinds of campaigns may be more deceptive than most due to the social engineering aspects of building trust over multiple legitimate interactions, the lures themselves still use many common techniques from other email themes. For example, Figure 2 shows a campaign that resulted in a response that sends a meeting invitation link that actually delivers GoTo RAT, a legitimate remote access tool that is a part of the LogMeIn management suite and is frequently abused by threat actors as a remote access trojan.

Figure 2: ATR 416570 contains a response to a long email thread with a sudden invitation to a meeting. However, the embedded link to the purported meeting site delivers GoTo RAT instead. This figure shows only the final reply, which contains the malicious link. The preceding thread has been omitted for length.

Similarly, message notification lures are also commonly seen within response-themed campaigns. Figure 3 shows a secure message notification-themed email that contains an embedded link to a purported message center. However, the site then requests verification to open the secure message by either accessing a Microsoft account credential phishing site or downloading ConnectWise RAT, a legitimate remote access tool also known as ConnectWise ScreenConnect that is currently one of the most frequently abused by threat actors as a remote access trojan.

Figure 3: ATR 418145 contains a response to an email thread with a secure message notification. The embedded link directs to either a Microsoft-spoofing credential phishing site or a ConnectWise RAT download. This figure shows only the final reply, which contains the malicious link. The preceding thread has been omitted for length.

Conclusions

The cause for concern with these campaigns is not necessarily the malware or credential phishing payloads but the way the threat actors build up trust through legitimate emails. Response-themed emails, by their very nature of being within seemingly harmless email threads, seek to gain a potential victim’s trust through social engineering techniques. Compromised email accounts can be used to send links to supposed “important documents” that actually lead to a credential phishing attack. Threat actors can email a potential victim with harmless messages over the span of several hours or even days before attempting to send a “meeting invite” that downloads malware. In both of these cases, the threat actors are relying on betraying trust that was built up via an existing credible name or a series of seemingly normal interactions.

Thankfully, writing email replies still takes more effort from the threat actor than simply spamming out hundreds or thousands of similarly structured email templates across a list of victims. If written to a legitimate email chain, these would require access to a compromised email account that happens to have an email thread. The threat actor would then need to write a response with a hook that would be relevant to the thread (such as a meeting invitation). If the threat actor wants to start the email thread, then they would need to wait for a potential victim to respond and write replies to them. While email responses can be automated through generative AI solutions, allowing this campaign pattern to be scaled up to a broader potential attack surface, response-themed campaigns are generally limited to being highly targeted in nature, whether through opportunistically replying to existing threads in compromised email inboxes or creating new threads from scratch. These factors make response-themed emails rare compared to other campaign types.

For leadership, the core message is straightforward: a trusted sender and a familiar email thread are not necessarily proof that a message is safe. These kinds of attack patterns highlight the importance of carefully reading and assessing emails for potential threats, even within established email threads with known contacts. Any message within a thread may contain a malicious threat, so recipients should always stay aware of potentially manipulative messages that may be delivering unknown links, strange attachments, or other potential threats. A message that asks you to click a link, open an attachment, or log in deserves a second look no matter whose name is on it.

Mitigations

While traditional email security detections based off trusted senders, established contacts, and other known good signals may fail to filter these kinds of campaigns, email security solutions that continuously scan for suspect behavior and analyze malicious links and attachments in a sandbox environment may be the most reliable way of filtering these attacks. In particular, behavioral detections that flag sudden geographic shifts from the sender and potentially malicious requests may be better at handling this attack pattern.

Ultimately, the best defense against these kinds of attacks is training and awareness of potential email threats. While these campaigns feature their malicious payloads within email thread replies, they often include common phishing lures such as meeting invitations or documents that need to be reviewed. The only major difference is that response-themed emails can be more targeted and tailored to a potential victim based on responses within the thread and the amount of time involved in establishing and then exploiting trust. However, once the malicious email is sent, it will invariably be similar to what most malicious emails look like. With proper training and awareness of common email phishing techniques, recipients should be able to recognize potentially suspect emails. However, the real challenge is applying constant vigilance with familiar contacts or otherwise harmless emails. When receiving potentially malicious emails, consider validating the contents of the email out-of-band with the sender, especially if they are a known and trusted contact. While doing so, be sure to rely on contact information gathered from outside of the email itself because threat actors can also easily modify signature blocks as a part of their attack.

When developing better preventative measures against these attacks, consider implementing the following as a part of training and standard security operations:

  • Update employee security awareness training to reflect how these campaigns actually arrive: as replies inside existing email threads, often from a known contact whose account has been compromised, ending in a meeting invitation, a shared document or file link, or a secure message notification. Employees trained on real, current threats are more likely to pause before clicking, even when the message comes from a familiar name. Simulation exercises should reproduce this exact pattern, a malicious reply within an ongoing thread, rather than outdated generic examples.
  • Establish and enforce a software allowlist for remote access tools. Response-themed campaigns frequently deliver legitimate remote access tools that have been repurposed as malware, including ConnectWise RAT. Any remote access tool not on the approved list should be blocked from installing on corporate devices. Organizations without an allowlist should at minimum block the digital certificates associated with remote access tools they do not use.
  • Deploy enterprise password managers. When an employee follows a malicious reply to a credential phishing page, the password manager will refuse to fill credentials because the domain does not match the legitimate service. This gives a structural catch that works no matter how convincing the branding or how trusted the thread appears, and it complements employee training rather than replacing it.
  • Deploy email security that looks for behavioral anomalies inside otherwise trusted threads, rather than relying on sender reputation alone. Because these emails often come from legitimate or compromised accounts, the sending domain is frequently valid, so brand and domain mismatch checks catch little. Signals that do help include a known sender suddenly sending from an unusual location, or a long-running thread that abruptly introduces a link or attachment.
  • Use tools and software provided by Cofense such as Triage and Vision to prevent initial access and stop follow-on attacks. Triage gives security teams an in-depth breakdown of a reported phishing email, which makes a malicious reply buried in a legitimate thread easier to analyze and act on. Vision uses human insight and AI precision to quarantine and remove malicious emails from inboxes, including messages that reached users from a trusted or compromised sender.
  • Give employees a simple, one-click way to report suspicious emails, which is exactly what Cofense Triage and Vision are built for. Because these campaigns often target multiple recipients from the same infrastructure, an employee who reports a suspicious reply quickly gives security teams the chance to block that infrastructure before others click. A well-trained employee who flags a response-themed email is a detection tool no automated system can replicate.
